content: It is also possible to relate immune marker titres to disease risk and VE without assuming a specific threshold titre for protection. This approach was used to infer the overall proportion of individuals protected against disease. For example, Chan et al. examined various regression models to assess the relationship between antibody titres following varicella vaccination and subsequent disease incidence, aiming to infer clinical protection. Storsaeter et al. This model was later validated by Kohberger et al. using Prentice criteria and meta-analysis. The VE predicted by the model was consistent with results from a second vaccine trial in Sweden. However, Dunning highlighted the limitations of existing models in accurately capturing the relationship between antibody titres and clinical protection, particularly in individuals with low antibody titres. This approach has since been applied to model the relationship between cell-mediated immune (CMI) responses to influenza vaccination in children and protection against culture-confirmed clinical infection with wild-type influenza virus. The relationship between immune markers and VE can be assessed using different methods. Some approaches treat antibody titres as continuous variables to predict VE, while others dichotomize the data into a threshold level above which individuals are considered protected and below which they are not. Both methods have limitations. For instance, stratifying on immune response can introduce post-randomization bias in randomized trials. Adjustments for confounding factors unrelated to the vaccine are necessary to account for infection or disease risk. The relationship between immune marker titres and clinical protection is further discussed in subsequent sections. It is critical to explicitly define the clinical endpoint against which a vaccine is expected to protect, as the relationship between immune markers and protection may vary depending on the outcome. Endpoints of interest include infection, illness, death, carriage, infectiousness, and, for diseases like malaria, time to the first endpoint or the total number of disease episodes. Protection against clinical endpoints may require different quantities of a specific immune marker or involve different markers altogether. For example, studies on the smallpox vaccine suggest that high antibody titres protect against infection, but both antibody and T-cell responses are needed to protect against severe disease. For instance, changes in the immune system over the lifespan, including the acquisition and loss of maternal antibodies, immune competence maturation, and immunosenescence, can alter the components of the immune response important for protection. Environmental factors, including climate and regional differences, may further influence vaccine performance. The type of antibody and its functional activity are important considerations when assessing immune markers as surrogate endpoints for VE. Regulatory bodies often prefer measuring functional antibodies, such as those with opsonophagocytic activity, over total antibody levels, as this provides greater biological plausibility for the association between immune markers and clinical protection. Finally, the interpretation of vaccine-induced protection can follow either an all-or-none model or a partial model. In the all-or-none model, a certain proportion of vaccine recipients achieve a threshold level of immune response and are fully protected, while the remainder are not protected at all. In contrast, the partial model assumes that all vaccine recipients experience a proportional reduction in disease incidence. These models have implications for understanding the relationship between immune markers, clinical endpoints, and VE.
